summary: For ages 9–10, teach senses, brain and responses as a three-stage information system: a stimulus is DETECTED by a sense organ (receptor), the BRAIN processes the information, and the body RESPONDS. The target skill (per NGSS 4-LS1-2) is to USE a model of this input→processing→output pathway, not just recite it. Children build and operate the pathway, compare specialised animal senses (bat echolocation, dog smell, bird magnetic sense, snake/spider vibration), and see that the SAME stimulus can produce DIFFERENT responses in different animals because the brain is the processor that interprets and decides. Keep the brain a 'black box' — receptor biochemistry and memory/recall mechanisms are out of scope.
misconceptions: Thinking the sense organ itself 'decides' the response, rather than the brain processing information between input and output.
Believing humans have exactly five senses and other animals sense the world the same way, missing specialised senses like echolocation or magnetoreception.
Assuming a stimulus always produces the same fixed response, overlooking that different animals (and contexts) yield different responses.
Conflating 'senses' with the response itself (e.g. thinking 'flinching' is a sense) rather than seeing detection, processing and response as distinct stages.
Thinking the brain 'stores' the response like a recording — memory/recall mechanisms are beyond this model's scope and shouldn't be assumed.

activities.title: Operate the signal pathway and swap the animal
steps: Trigger a stimulus (a firework bang, food smell, a flash of light) and trace the signal travelling from the sense organ (ear/nose/eye) to the brain, then to the body's response (freeze, run, turn to look).

In the model, fire the SAME loud bang at different animals and compare the example responses shown: for example, a rabbit may bolt, a person may cover their ears, and a dog may bark or hide. These are example responses only. Real animals vary with the individual and the situation.
State in your own words where the 'decision' about the response is made, and why the same sound led to different actions.
In a 'build-the-pathway' mode, put the stages in order: stimulus → receptor (sense organ) → brain → response.
activities.insight: The brain is a processor sitting between input and output; sense organs only detect and send information, and because each animal's brain handles the information differently, one stimulus can lead to different responses.

activities.title: Map sense organs and uncover specialised animal senses
steps: For each sense organ, name the information it detects: eye→light, ear→sound, nose→smell, skin→touch, tongue→taste.

Investigate specialised senses beyond the human five: how a bat finds its way in the dark using echolocation (hearing echoes of its own calls), how a dog relies on smell, how many migrating birds use a magnetic sense, how a snake or spider senses vibration.

Reveal a myth-buster: not all animals share the same five senses. Some animals have senses humans lack, such as echolocation or a magnetic sense. Even humans have more than the traditional five, for example balance and a sense of body position. Receptors are specialised for particular kinds of information.
activities.insight: Different sense receptors are specialised for particular kinds of information, and animals do not all sense the world the same way, yet they all follow the stimulus→brain→response pattern.

activities.title: Feel your own reaction-time loop (dropped-ruler test)
steps: One child holds a ruler vertically; the partner's fingers wait open at the zero mark ready to catch it when it is released without warning.
Before trying, PREDICT whether you can catch it the instant it is released, and explain why or why not.
Run several catches, note roughly how many centimetres slip past before you catch it, and discuss what the gap shows.
activities.insight: There is a processing delay: the signal must travel from the eye to the brain, be processed, and travel back to the muscles — you cannot respond instantly, which shows the brain sits between sensing and responding.

activities.title: Explain and consolidate: order the pathway and answer the discriminating case
steps: Put the stages of the pathway in order: stimulus → sense organ (receptor) → brain → response.
Match each animal to its special sense (bat→echolocation, dog→smell, migrating bird→magnetic sense, snake/spider→vibration).

Answer: a rabbit and a deer both hear the exact same twig snap; the rabbit freezes and the deer bolts. They received the same sound — so why did they do different things, and what must happen between the ears hearing the snap and the body moving?
Draw the journey of the twig-snap information from the forest to the animal responding, labelling each stage.
activities.insight: A full explanation identifies the brain-processing step as the reason the same input can produce different outputs, and applies the pathway to a new animal or sense.

activities.title: Talk with an animal or scientist about how they sense the world
steps: Interview an in-role persona (a neuroscientist, or a bat, dog or bird 'speaking' about its senses) with questions such as 'what information can you detect that I can't?' and 'what happens after you sense something?'
Retell what you learned as the stimulus→sense organ→brain→response pathway for that animal, including the response.
activities.insight: Even across very different animals and senses, the same input→processing→output pattern holds, and curiosity about diverse senses can deepen the systems idea.

checkQuestion: A rabbit and a deer both hear the exact same twig snap in the forest. The rabbit freezes still, but the deer bolts away. They received the very same sound — so why did they do different things? What must be happening between the ears hearing the snap and the body moving?
checkAnswer: The ears detect the sound (the stimulus), but the brain processes and interprets it and decides the response. Because each animal's brain (and body) handles the information differently, the same stimulus can lead to different responses. The pathway is stimulus → brain processing → response, with a decision step in the middle.
